analysis.one_liner: Targets federal inspections, health screening, and pollution cleanup at the 20 most toxic-burdened communities.
analysis.headline: A bill to force inspections and health studies in the 20 most chemical-burdened communities was sent to four House committees, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the EPA to name the 20 counties or areas with the highest levels of toxic chemical exposure, then inspect every toxic chemical facility in those areas within a year. It would have funded a federal health study comparing disease rates in those areas to elsewhere, banned new toxic facilities in areas shown to be harming residents' health, and paid for free medical screening, pollution reduction, and new parks in affected communities.
analysis.who_benefits: People living in the most heavily polluted communities — typically low-income neighborhoods and communities of color near chemical plants, waste sites, and highways. They would get mandatory facility inspections, a federal study of local cancer, birth defect, and respiratory disease rates, free screening and treatment for environmentally related illnesses, community grants to hire independent experts, pollution reduction programs, and funding for parks and green space.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the EPA to publish a list of 20 Environmental High Impact Areas — places with high chemical levels and documented human exposure — and update it every five years.
Requires the EPA and OSHA to inspect or review every toxic chemical facility in those areas within one year of each list being published.

Directs HHS to study whether rates of cancer, birth defects, infant mortality, and respiratory disease are worse in those areas, and to share the findings directly with residents and tribal governments.

Bars the siting or permitting of any new toxic chemical facility in an area shown to have significant adverse health impacts, unless the facility proves it will not harm health and will minimize uncontrolled releases.
Funds community-wide medical screening and diagnostic services for environmentally related illnesses, with treatment for uninsured residents continuing as long as medically necessary.
Provides grants for pollution reduction strategies, technical assistance so residents can hire independent experts, and development of parks and recreational spaces.

analysis.who_pays: Chemical manufacturers, hazardous waste handlers, and other facility operators in the designated areas, who would face mandatory inspections, pollution reduction requirements, and a possible ban on new facilities. Taxpayers generally would fund the grants, since the bill authorizes 'such sums as may be necessary.' Some compliance costs could be passed to consumers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Chemical and waste facility operators, taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The siting moratorium could block new industrial facilities and the jobs they bring in the very communities that need investment, even if a new plant would be cleaner than existing ones.

The bill authorizes unlimited spending ('such sums as may be necessary') with no revenue source, leaving the cost of inspections, health studies, screening grants, and parks entirely to annual appropriations.

The definition of 'toxic chemicals' sweeps in everything from pesticides to drinking-water pollutants, which could require inspections and reviews of far more facilities than the 20-area framing suggests.
Designating an area a federal 'high impact zone' could stigmatize it, potentially depressing property values and complicating economic development there.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people in the affected communities the benefits would be substantial: mandatory inspections of facilities near their homes, an honest federal accounting of local health harms, free screening and treatment, and pollution cleanup. The costs fall mostly on the regulated facilities and on taxpayers. The moratorium is the bluntest tool in the bill — a blunt pause on new facilities could trade jobs for health protection — but it only applies in areas where a federal health study already found significant harm.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to four House committees and split among five subcommittees, where it sat without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote until the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. John Lewis of Georgia introduced the Environmental Justice Act of 1999 on April 21, 1999, joined by 23 Democratic cosponsors.
The Speaker referred it to four committees at once — Commerce, Transportation and Infrastructure, Agriculture, and Resources — splitting it among their jurisdictions.
Within weeks it was divided among five subcommittees, including Health and Environment, Water Resources, and Finance and Hazardous Materials.
No committee ever held a hearing or markup, and the House never voted on it; the bill died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2001.
Under the bill, the EPA would have designated 20 'Environmental High Impact Areas' and every toxic chemical facility there would have faced a mandatory compliance inspection within a year.

The bill would also have imposed a moratorium on new toxic facilities in areas where a federal study found significant health harm, and funded free health screening and pollution reduction in those communities.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Operators of chemical and waste facilities avoided the mandatory inspections, potential new-facility ban, and pollution reduction mandates. Residents of the most polluted communities — the bill's intended beneficiaries — gained nothing, and the health studies and screening the bill promised never happened.

for.name: Rep. John Lewis
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: 23 House Democrats
for.role: Original cosponsors, including Reps. Conyers, Pelosi, Waters, and Norton
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; none was a Republican.

against.name: House Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee of primary referral (106th Congress)
against.what_they_did: The primary committee never held a hearing or markup; the bill sat in subcommittees until the Congress ended.

against.name: Chemical manufacturing industry
against.role: Operators of the toxic chemical facilities the bill would have inspected and restricted
against.what_they_did: Industry groups opposed mandatory-inspection and siting-moratorium mandates in environmental justice legislation during this era, and the bill's approach targeted their facilities directly.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a House Democrat — 24 members in all — and no Republican support appears anywhere in the record; with Republicans controlling the House committees that received the bill, it never advanced.

industries.industry: Chemical manufacturers and toxic chemical facility operators
industries.note: The bill would have mandated inspections of every toxic facility in the 20 designated areas, allowed regulators to force pollution reductions, and barred new toxic facilities in areas shown to be harming health. Its interests ran against residents of those areas, who bear the pollution.

industries.industry: Hazardous waste treatment and disposal facilities
industries.note: Waste facilities fall under the bill's definition of toxic chemical facilities and would face the same mandatory inspections and, in affected areas, a siting moratorium on new permits.

industries.industry: Community health clinics and nonprofit health providers
industries.note: The bill would fund grant programs for community-wide medical screening and treatment of environmentally related illnesses, channeled through public and nonprofit providers in the designated areas.
Technical assistance grants would pay residents to seek guidance from independent experts, creating paid work for environmental and health professionals in affected communities.
